mcqs.q: Dentin forms the:
opts: Main bulk of the tooth (covered by enamel in the crown, cementum in the root)
Outer covering of the crown only
mcqs.explain: Dentin is the mineralized tissue forming the main bulk of the tooth; enamel covers it in the crown and cementum in the root.

mcqs.q: Two properties that distinguish dentin from enamel are that dentin is:
mcqs.explain: Unlike enamel, dentin is sensitive and continues to be formed throughout life.

mcqs.q: The hardness of dentin is:
opts: Less than enamel but more than cementum and bone
mcqs.explain: Dentin is harder than cementum and bone but softer than enamel; it is visco-elastic and light yellowish.

mcqs.q: Compared with enamel, dentin is:
opts: More radiolucent than enamel (and more radiopaque than cementum)
mcqs.explain: On X-ray, dentin is more radiolucent than enamel but more radiopaque than cementum.

mcqs.q: The inorganic content of dentin is about:
mcqs.explain: Dentin is ~70% inorganic (hydroxyapatite) and ~30% organic and water; enamel is ~96% inorganic.

mcqs.q: The main organic component of dentin is:
opts: Collagen type I (90% of the organic matrix)
mcqs.explain: Collagen type I makes up ~90% of dentin's organic matrix, with non-collagenous proteins, glycoproteins and lipids.

mcqs.q: Odontoblasts differentiate from:
opts: Peripheral cells of the dental papilla
mcqs.explain: Odontoblasts differentiate from peripheral dental-papilla cells; they elongate (~40 µm) and become closely packed.

mcqs.q: The unmineralized organic matrix first laid down by odontoblasts is called:
mcqs.explain: Odontoblasts first secrete predentin (collagen + ground substance), which is later mineralized into dentin.

mcqs.q: The single odontoblastic process left within a dentinal tubule is the:
mcqs.explain: As dentin is laid down, the odontoblast recedes leaving a single process (Tomes' fibre) within the dentinal tubule. (Tomes' PROCESS belongs to ameloblasts.)

mcqs.q: The FIRST-formed layer of dentin, with fibres perpendicular to the DEJ, is:
mcqs.explain: Mantle dentin (10–20 µm) is the first layer, with large collagen fibres perpendicular to the DEJ and linear mineralization.

mcqs.q: Circumpulpal dentin (the bulk of dentin) has collagen fibres that are:
opts: Fine and parallel to the dentin surface (DEJ)
Large and perpendicular to the DEJ
mcqs.explain: Circumpulpal dentin forms the bulk, with fine collagen fibres parallel to the DEJ and globular (then mixed) mineralization.

mcqs.q: Mineralization of dentin begins by:
opts: Budding and rupture of matrix vesicles releasing calcium/phosphate
mcqs.explain: Mantle dentin mineralizes via matrix vesicles (rich in alkaline phosphatase) that bud, rupture and seed crystallization.

mcqs.q: The odontoblast layer in the crown (pulp chamber) is:
mcqs.explain: Odontoblasts are pseudostratified columnar in the crown, columnar at the root canal mouth, cuboidal mid-root and flat apically.

mcqs.q: The periodontoblastic space contains:
opts: Dentinal fluid (the soft tissue of dentin)
mcqs.explain: The periodontoblastic space (between the process and tubule wall) is filled with dentinal fluid; the process + this space are the soft tissue of dentin.

mcqs.q: Dentinal tubules taper:
opts: From the pulpal surface outwards (wider near pulp)
mcqs.explain: Dentinal tubules taper from the pulpal surface outward; they give lateral branches (permeability) and terminal branches forming a plexus beneath the DEJ.

mcqs.q: The lateral branches of the odontoblastic process are responsible for:
mcqs.explain: Lateral branches unite with those of adjacent processes and are responsible for dentin permeability.

mcqs.q: Peritubular (intratubular) dentin is:
opts: A highly calcified ring lining the tubule (~40% more mineral)
mcqs.explain: Peritubular dentin is a highly calcified zone lining the tubule wall (~40% more mineralized); it is laid down continuously, narrowing the tubule.

mcqs.q: Intertubular dentin:
opts: Lies between the tubules and forms the main bulk of dentin
Is found only at the apex
mcqs.explain: Intertubular dentin (fine collagen + apatite) lies between the tubules and forms the main bulk of dentin (mantle + circumpulpal).

mcqs.q: Interglobular dentin represents:
opts: Hypomineralized areas where calcified globules failed to fuse
mcqs.explain: Where mineralizing globules fail to fuse, the matrix between them stays uncalcified/partially mineralized — interglobular dentin (tubules cross it without peritubular dentin).

mcqs.q: Interglobular dentin is typically found in the:
opts: Crown, just below the mantle dentin
mcqs.explain: Interglobular dentin appears in the crown just below the mantle dentin (and in root dentin of badly formed teeth).

mcqs.q: Tomes' granular layer is found:
opts: In the root dentin adjacent to the cementum
mcqs.explain: Tomes' granular layer is a small granular zone in the root dentin adjacent to the cementum, due to looping of the terminal tubules (tubules do not cross it).

mcqs.q: The incremental lines of von Ebner represent a growth cycle of:
mcqs.explain: The lines of von Ebner mark a 5-day incremental cycle (~20 µm apart); they are areas of hypocalcification.

mcqs.q: The accentuated incremental line in dentin that marks birth is the:
mcqs.explain: The neonatal line marks the environmental/metabolic change at birth in dentin (present in deciduous teeth and first permanent molars).

mcqs.q: The course of the dentinal tubules at the cusp tip/incisal edge is:
mcqs.explain: Dentinal tubules show an S-shaped course at the cusp tip/incisal edge and cervical area, becoming straight in the mid-root and apically.

mcqs.q: Dentin is studied histologically as:
opts: Both a ground section (inorganic) and a decalcified section (organic)
mcqs.explain: Unlike enamel, dentin can be studied as a ground section (inorganic part) AND a decalcified section (organic part).

mcqs.q: Accentuated incremental lines (contour lines of Owen) in dentin denote:
mcqs.explain: Contour lines of Owen are accentuated incremental lines reflecting disturbances in mineralization, e.g. periods of illness or inadequate nutrition.

saqs.q: Give the physical and chemical properties of dentin.
saqs.a: Light yellowish, visco-elastic, harder than cementum/bone but softer than enamel; more radiolucent than enamel; semi-permeable. ~70% inorganic (hydroxyapatite), ~30% organic — collagen type I (90%).

saqs.q: Outline the four steps of dentin development.
saqs.a: 1. Odontoblast differentiation (from dental papilla). 2. Predentin formation (protein-secreting cell). 3. Odontoblastic process (single Tomes' fibre). 4. Quiescent state.
Mantle: first 10–20 µm, large fibres perpendicular to DEJ, linear mineralization. Circumpulpal: bulk, fine fibres parallel to DEJ, globular → mixed mineralization.

saqs.q: Describe the dentinal tubule and periodontoblastic space.
saqs.a: The tubule contains the odontoblastic process (Tomes' fibre); it tapers outward with lateral (permeability) and terminal (plexus) branches. The periodontoblastic space holds dentinal fluid — the soft tissue of dentin.
Peritubular (intratubular): highly calcified ring lining the tubule (~40% more mineral), narrows it. Intertubular: between tubules, the main bulk (collagen + apatite).

saqs.q: Contrast interglobular dentin and Tomes' granular layer.
saqs.a: Interglobular dentin: hypomineralized areas (globules failed to fuse), in the crown below mantle; tubules cross it. Tomes' granular layer: granular zone in the root near cementum (looping terminal tubules).

saqs.q: List the incremental lines of dentin.
saqs.a: Lines of von Ebner (5-day, ~20 µm cycle), the neonatal line (birth), and the contour lines of Owen (accentuated, mark disturbed mineralization).
